domain: Goddess of War and the Hunt
meaning: Canaanite warrior goddess, sister and ally of Baꜥal

phonemes.desc: Voiced pharyngeal fricative [ʕ] — a deep, tightening sound in the throat, followed by open [a]. The Egyptian Ain (ꜥ) is used as the registrable stand-in.
Plain alveolar sounds: [n], [a], [t]. The final -t is a feminine marker, common in Semitic divine names.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AH-naht' — start with a rough, throaty 'ah' (like Arabic ع), then 'naht' with a crisp final t.

kin.label: Ugaritic
kin.form: 𐎓𐎐𐎚 (ʿnt), the warrior goddess's name in the alphabetic cuneiform of Ras Shamra

kin.label: Hebrew
kin.form: עֲנָת (ʿĂnāt), attested as a place and divine name; the name is not etymologically transparent

kin.label: Egyptian
kin.form: ꜥnt(t), an early loan/adaptation showing her cult reached the Nile Delta

pronunciation.note: The ideal spelling would use Semitic ʿayin (ʿ), but that character is rejected by the DNS root zone. We therefore render the pharyngeal with the Egyptological Ain (ꜥ, U+A724), the only registrable Unicode workaround that signals the original consonant. The name is Tier 1: it preserves the ʿayin (a distinctive phoneme) — a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses.

domains.title: Maiden of Battles
domains.subtitle: War, Hunt, and Ferocious Loyalty
domains.lead: ꜥAnat is the maiden who refuses the domestic sphere. In the Ugaritic texts she is neither wife nor mother but a singular force: a warrior who wades knee-deep in the blood of her enemies, a huntress of the open country, and the most faithful ally of Baꜥal. Her title btlt — 'maiden' — marks her as marriageable, yet mythologically she remains unattached, unpredictable, and absolutely devoted to her brother.

cards.name: Divine Warfare
cards.desc: She fights both armies and cosmic foes, wielding bow, spear, and sword; KTU 1.3 ii describes her battle fury in graphic detail.

cards.name: The Hunt
cards.desc: She ranges mountains and heights in search of game or vengeance; her pursuit of Aqhat turns the hunt into tragic myth.

cards.name: Loyal Sister
cards.desc: Baꜥal's most passionate advocate; she confronts El, avenges Baꜥal's death, and restores the storm to the world.

cards.name: Unbound Feminine Power
cards.desc: A young woman operating in male-coded spheres without condemnation — a figure of autonomous, even terrifying, agency.

symbols.name: Bow
symbols.meaning: The peerless bow of Aqhat — she would kill for it, and the land paid the price (KTU 1.17–19)

symbols.name: Spear and sword
symbols.meaning: The blade she turned on Mot itself, splitting death like a stalk of grain (KTU 1.6 ii)

symbols.name: Lion
symbols.meaning: Her leonine ferocity; Day reads her as Ugarit's Mistress of Animals (JNES 51, 1992)

symbols.name: Dew and rain
symbols.meaning: Baꜥal's cleansing gift after battle — war purified by the storm's water (KTU 1.3 ii)

mythology.lead: ꜥAnat's mythology is preserved chiefly in the Ugaritic Baꜥal Cycle and the Epic of Aqhat. She is not a fertility goddess in the usual sense; she is force itself, concentrated in a young woman's body, and her stories turn on violence, loyalty, and the refusal to accept limits.

myths.title: Wading Knee-Deep in Blood
myths.text: The most famous portrait of ꜥAnat is a battlefield after the killing is done (KTU 1.3 ii). She stands in her house, her garments spattered, and boasts over her work: 'heads rolled beneath her like balls, the hands of warriors flew over her like locusts.' In exultation she fastens the severed heads to her back and hangs the men's hands on her belt, then sits down to her own victory rite — she slaughters her captives 'beneath her like lambs.' When the gore is spent she washes herself, not in water alone but in the dew of heaven that Baꜥal, the Rider on the Clouds, sends down upon her. The scene appalls and fascinates in equal measure: war here is not grim duty but ecstasy, and the dew that cleanses her comes from her brother, binding her violence to the storm's life-giving water. Destruction and fertility are the two hands of one goddess.

myths.title: The Sowing of Mot
myths.text: When Mōt swallows Baꜥal, ꜥAnat becomes the myth's destroyer of death itself. She ranges the earth searching for her brother; finding him dead, she gives him burial on Zaphon and turns her full ferocity on the god who took him (KTU 1.6 ii). She seizes Mot and works him like a harvest: 'with a sword she splits him, with a sieve she winnows him, with fire she burns him, with millstones she grinds him, in a field she scatters him.' Every verb is a verb of threshing — splitting, winnowing, grinding, scattering — so that the annihilation of death is cast as the harvest it had interrupted. Baꜥal returns, and the rains return with him. The portrait redeems the earlier horror: the ferocity that seemed an excess on the battlefield proves to be the world's repair mechanism. Only an unbounded love, the myth says, is equal to an unbounded appetite — and only a sister could do this work.

myths.title: The Bow and the Refusal
myths.text: The Epic of Aqhat turns on a gift and a refusal. Kothar-wa-Ḫasīs gives the young hero Aqhat a bow without equal, and ꜥAnat covets it. She offers him silver and gold; he refuses. She offers him the one prize gods cannot truly give — 'years like Baꜥal's, life like the sons of El' — and Aqhat answers with a line the tradition never forgave: bows are for men, not for women. Enraged, the goddess flies to the Sutean warrior Yatpan and, in a disguise the poem savors, orders Aqhat's death. The plan miscarries catastrophically: the marvelous bow is shattered, the land is cursed with drought, and Aqhat's sister Pughat — the poem's quiet, formidable heroine — sets out after Yatpan. The text breaks off before her revenge is complete. Even so, the poem's judgment is plain in its ruined harvest: to deny a goddess her due, whether her honor or her weapon, is to let the whole world dry out.

myths.title: Mistress of the Highlands
myths.text: A single fragmentary hymn (KTU 1.13) opens a quieter window on the goddess: the poet sings of Anat the maiden, of the beauty and bounty of the highlands where she roams. Though badly broken, the tablet shows her invoked in blessing — a guardian of her devotees and a power of the open country rather than the city wall, matching her role in the Aqhat epic as a huntress of mountain and steppe. Peggy Day's study of the goddess read her as Ugarit's Mistress of Animals, heir to a Bronze Age tradition of the woman who stands among lions and controls the game, and the fragment coheres with that reading. The hymn matters because almost everything else we have of ꜥAnat is violence; here, at the edge of a broken tablet, is the goddess invoked the way a patron is invoked — for protection, for plenty, for the favor of one who has never learned to be mild.

lore.syncretism: In Egypt, ꜥAnat was worshipped as a war goddess alongside her sister Aštart, especially at Tanis and Memphis; she appears on scarabs and in the Egyptian pantheon as ꜥnt(t). Greeks and Romans later identified her with Athena/Minerva in her martial aspect. Some scholars have argued for an early equation with the Mesopotamian Ishtar/Inanna, since both are young, autonomous warrior goddesses, but the Ugaritic texts treat ꜥAnat as a distinct Levantine figure. In the Hebrew Bible, place names such as Anathoth preserve her memory without endorsing her cult.
lore.culturalLegacy: The name ꜥAnat echoes across millennia in unexpected ways. The Israelite town of Anathoth (Jeremiah's birthplace) carries her name. Medieval Jewish folklore remembered her in the figure of the warrior woman, and modern Levantine archaeology has recovered countless amulets and plaques bearing her image. In contemporary literature, film, and Neopagan practice, Anat resurfaces as an icon of untamed female power — a goddess who will not be domesticated, who fights for those she loves, and who makes the boundaries between love and violence uncomfortably thin.
lore.extendedMeditation:
ꜥAnat disturbs the modern imagination because she refuses our categories. She is a young woman and a killer, a sister and an avenger, a goddess of life-giving rain and of blood-soaked battlefields. In a world that still struggles to imagine female power without apology, she stands as a difficult ancestor: not a nurturer, not a consort, but a self-possessed force.

Yet her loyalty is unmistakable. Everything she does for Baꜥal — confronting El, destroying Mot, mourning in the wilderness — she does out of love that does not negotiate. To meditate on ꜥAnat is to meditate on the sacredness of rage rightly aimed, on the ferocity that protects rather than merely consumes. She asks us: What would you fight for, without limit, without consent, because it is yours?
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is written in Ugaritic alphabetic cuneiform as 𐎓𐎐𐎚 (ʿ-n-t). The first sign is ʿayin, a voiced pharyngeal fricative absent from English and from standard Latin transcription. Because the standard IPA ʿ is blocked at the DNS root, PUNICODEX represents it with the Latin Capital/Small Letter Egyptological Ain (ꜥ / U+A724), preserving visual recognition while remaining registrable.

lore.archaeology: The Ugaritic tablets from Ras Shamra (KTU 1.3, 1.6, 1.17–19) preserve her warrior mythology in alphabetic cuneiform. In Egypt, bronze figurines and scarabs from Tanis, Memphis, and the eastern Delta identify her as ꜥnt(t), a Levantine war goddess absorbed into the New Kingdom pantheon. The stela from Beth-Shean and Israelite place names such as Anathoth and the epithet Shamgar ben-Anath attest her cult west of the Jordan.
